reading.body:
Of five privacy and data protection postings, four are legal, policy, or program roles and only one is a research engineering job, which suggests AI firms are buying compliance capacity rather than privacy technology.

The pattern is jurisdictional. Harvey lists the same title, Privacy and AI Counsel EMEA, twice, once for Dublin and once for London. Both carry a remote flag, but each is tied to a named city, so the remote work is likely scoped to a legal jurisdiction rather than location independent. OpenAI's Research Engineer, Privacy is the only posting in the set that builds anything, and it is also the oldest, posted 2026-07-14 against September dates for the rest. Figure's Technical Program Manager, Security & Privacy sits in San Jose, and the Goodwin Recruiting listing is the only one with pay attached, $240,000 to $325,000 a year for a privacy, cybersecurity and technology attorney in Grand Rapids.

For AI specifically, this reads as firms staffing the legal perimeter of data handling, not the engineering of it. Two of the five postings are the same company hiring the same counsel role in two European jurisdictions, which is what a company does when the constraint is regulatory exposure per market rather than a shortage of privacy-preserving technique. The single research engineering role is the exception that shows the technical work exists, not that it is the center of gravity in this function.

What this does not cover is volume or direction. Five postings from aggregators and company career boards cannot establish whether privacy hiring is rising or falling, whether these are new roles or backfills, or how privacy compares with other functions. It says nothing about compute, buildings, or power, and no conclusion about data center capacity should be drawn from it. Salary appears once, so pay for the other four is unknown.
